full_document.answer:
GlossBERT handles a variable number of senses per word by constructing context-gloss pairs from the glosses of all possible senses of the target word in WordNet, treating WSD as a sentence-pair classification problem. [1][2]
For each target word, the glosses of all N possible senses are extracted to form gloss sentences, and [CLS]/[SEP] marks are added to make each context-gloss pair suitable as BERT input. [3]
Each target word therefore has N context-gloss pair training instances with labels in {yes, no}. [4]
At test time, the model outputs the probability of label=yes for each context-gloss pair and selects the sense corresponding to the highest probability as the prediction for the target word. [4]
The three GlossBERT variants classify each context-gloss pair: GlossBERT(Token-CLS) uses the final hidden state of the target-word token (averaged if multiple tokens), GlossBERT(Sent-CLS) uses the [CLS] token, and GlossBERT(Sent-CLS-WS) uses [CLS] with weak supervision highlighting the target. 模型采用两阶段解码器流程，生成摘要中的每个词时会同时考虑两侧的上下文信息。 [3][4]
训练时，模型的目标是两个过程之和，使用“teacher-forcing”算法联合训练；训练中把真实摘要（ground-truth summary）输入每个解码器并最小化目标。 [5][6]
模型总损失记为 L_model = L̂_dec + L̂_refine（式23）。 [7]
训练设置：batch size 为36，训练4个epoch（NYT50因训练样本少得多而用8个epoch），训练后根据开发集表现从最后10个模型中选出最佳模型。 [8][9]
由于GPU显存限制，使用梯度累积，累积步数为12，每步输入3个样本。 [10][9]
使用Adam优化器，学习率3e-4，β1=0.9、β2=0.999、ε=10^-9，并在训练过程中使用动态学习率。 [11]
正则化方面使用dropout和label smoothing，dropout率为0.15、label smoothing值为0.1，RL目标因子γ设为0.99。 [12]
消融实验中的模型变体为：One-Stage（基于BERT、带copy机制的序列到序列模型）、Two-Stage（在One-Stage上加入word-refine解码器）、Two-Stage + RL（带refine过程并结合RL目标的完整模型）。 [13]

full_document.answer:
该模型采用两阶段解码：第一阶段由仅左上下文的解码器生成摘要草稿，第二阶段用精炼解码器逐词掩码并预测精炼词。 [1][2]
草稿阶段：BERT 编码器把输入文档编码为表示向量，N 层 Transformer 草稿解码器据此学习条件概率 P(A|H)，并以最小化负对数似然为学习目标。 [3][4][5][6][7]
精炼阶段：精炼解码器接收生成的摘要草稿，逐词掩码后送入 BERT 生成上下文向量，再由与草稿解码器相同的 N 层 Transformer 解码器预测精炼词，目标为式(19)的负对数似然。 [2][8][9]
草稿解码器与精炼解码器共享参数；作者称使用独立参数会使性能明显下降。 [10]
训练时模型目标是两个过程目标之和，使用 teacher-forcing 联合训练，训练中向每个解码器输入真实摘要并最小化目标。 [11][12]
此外还引入离散目标（策略梯度，奖励用 ROUGE-L）并与最大似然目标混合，草稿过程最终目标为混合后的 L̂_dec，精炼过程引入类似目标。 [13][14]
是，模型可端到端训练，无需手工特征。 [15]

retrieved_desktop.answer:
论文在第2节从三个视角讨论对话系统的研究现状：交互类型、架构类型和上下文推理类型，并用一张表汇总比较。 [1]
ELIZA（1966年，MIT，Weizenbaum）是最早理解自然语言的软件之一，以扮演心理治疗师著称，仅把病人的话反射回去；它旨在解决五个“基本技术问题”：识别关键词、发现最小上下文、选择适当变换、生成适当回应以及为脚本提供结束能力。 [2]
PARRY由斯坦福大学精神病学家Kenneth Colby在1970年代初开发，用MLISP语言在DEC PDP-10的WAITS系统上编写，代码不可移植；它是第一个通过图灵测试的系统——精神病学家仅48%的情况下能正确识别，与随机猜测相当。 [3]
A.L.I.C.E.出现于1995年，当前版本使用为刺激-反应聊天机器人设计的XML语言AIML，拥有超过40,000个知识类别（原版ELIZA仅约200个）；它无法通过图灵测试，普通用户在简短对话中就能看出其机械性。 [4]
Cleverbot（1997-2014）由英国AI科学家Rollo Carpenter开发，在2011年印度理工学院古瓦哈提分校举办的Techno-Management Festival上通过了图灵测试：四分钟打字对话中它被投票为59.3%像人，而人类自身仅63.3%。 [5]
在上下文推理方面，现有大多数方法依赖使用逻辑和知识库的规则（即面向规则的架构）。 [6]
开发此类系统的最新研究现状采用了循环神经网络（RNN）、动态上下文敏感生成和记忆网络等。 [7]
对于能参与多方对话的聊天机器人，其研究现状是聊天机器人创建研究与多智能体系统协调/治理研究的结合。 [8]
现有聊天机器人引擎不能妥善处理多用户、多机器人的群聊，缺乏将协调规则与自然语言结合的研究；二元聊天机器人不懂得在群组中协调，缺乏判断何时适合回答的社交能力。 [9][10]
作者称其提出的架构据其所知是研究现状中第一个旨在支持多方对话中协调感知聊天机器人设计与开发的架构；但论文并不旨在推进MPCS规范方面的研究现状。 [9][10]

retrieved_connector.answer:
论文按三个视角讨论对话系统的研究现状：交互类型、架构类型和上下文推理类型，并用一张表汇总比较。 [1]
在上下文推理方面，现有大多数方法依赖使用逻辑和知识库的规则（即规则导向架构）。 [2]
ELIZA（1966年，MIT，Weizenbaum）是最早的自然语言处理程序之一，以扮演心理治疗师著称，仅把病人的话反射回去；它旨在解决五个“基本技术问题”，包括关键词识别、最小上下文发现、变换选择、生成恰当回应以及为脚本提供结束能力。 [3][4]
PARRY由斯坦福大学精神病学家Kenneth Colby在1970年代初开发，用MLISP语言在DEC PDP-10的WAITS系统上编写，代码不可移植；它是首个通过图灵测试的系统（精神病学家仅48%正确识别，相当于随机猜测）。 [5][6][7]
A.L.I.C.E.于1995年出现，当前版本使用为刺激-反应聊天机器人设计的XML语言AIML，拥有超过4万个知识类别（ELIZA约200个）；但它无法通过图灵测试，随意用户短对话即可暴露其机械性。 [8][9][10]
Cleverbot（1997–2014）由英国AI科学家Rollo Carpenter开发，在2011年印度理工学院古瓦哈提技术节上通过图灵测试；志愿者四分钟打字对话中将其评为59.3%像人，而人类本身为63.3%。 [11][12][13]
多数现有聊天机器人（从最早的ELIZA到现代最先进的系统）都属于同一类别。 [14]
近期开发此类系统的最先进方法采用了循环神经网络（RNN）、动态上下文敏感生成和记忆网络等。 [15]
Sukhbaatar的工作综述了近期利用RNN或LSTM模型把对话上下文作为序列中长期结构来捕捉的研究现状。 [16]
SyntaxNet是运行于任务特定转换系统的前馈神经网络，在词性标注、依存句法分析和句子压缩上取得最先进结果。 [17]
对于多方对话聊天机器人的创建，当前现状是聊天机器人创建研究与多智能体系统协调/治理研究的结合；但聊天机器人引擎方面缺乏将协调规则与自然语言结合的研究，现有引擎无法妥善处理多用户多机器人的群聊。 [18][19][20]
作者称（据其所知）本文提出的架构是现状中首个支持多方对话中协调感知聊天机器人设计与开发的架构；本文并不旨在推进MPCS规范（norms）方面的现状。 [21][22]

annotated_passages.answer:
The paper reviews the state of the art on conversational systems from three perspectives: types of interactions, types of architecture, and types of context reasoning, and then consolidates and compares them in a table. [1]
ELIZA, created by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT in 1966, was one of the first software systems built to understand natural language processing; it acted like a psychotherapist and only reflected back the patient's statements. [2]
ELIZA was designed to tackle five fundamental technical problems: identifying critical words, discovering a minimal context, choosing appropriate transformations, generating appropriate responses (including in the absence of critical words), and providing an ending capacity for ELIZA scripts. [2]
PARRY, developed by Kenneth Colby at Stanford University in the early 1970s, was written in MLISP on the WAITS operating system running on a DEC PDP-10, with non-portable code partly in PDP-10 assembly and partly in MLISP. [3]
PARRY was reported as the first system to pass the Turing test, with psychiatrists correctly identifying it only 48 percent of the time, the same as random guessing. [3]
A.L.I.C.E. appeared in 1995 and its current version uses AIML, an XML language designed for creating stimulus-response chat robots. [4]
A.L.I.C.E. has more than 40,000 categories of knowledge, compared with only about 200 for the original ELIZA, but it is unable to pass the Turing test because casual users often expose its mechanistic aspects in short conversations. [4]
Cleverbot (1997-2014), developed by British AI scientist Rollo Carpenter, passed the 2011 Turing Test at a festival held by the Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati: in four-minute typed conversations, volunteers voted Cleverbot 59.3 percent human while the humans were rated 63.3 percent human. [5]

full_document.answer:
The paper organizes its state-of-the-art review of conversational systems into three perspectives: types of interactions, types of architecture, and types of context reasoning, then consolidates and compares them in a table. [1]
On interaction types, most existing chatbots—from ELIZA to modern state-of-the-art ones—are dyadic: they always try to reply to a received utterance and lack the social ability to know when to answer in a group. [2]
For multiparty chatbots, the state of the art is a combination of chatbot research and multi-agent coordination/governance research, but there is a lack of solutions for multiparty-aware or governed chatbots. [3]
Turn-taking in multiparty conversation was studied by Sacks et al., who found participants generally do not overlap utterances and that transition-relevance places and selected-next-speaker cues structure turns; detecting these remains a challenge for speech-based systems. [4][5]
Bohus and Horowitz proposed a computational probabilistic model for turn-taking in speech-based systems, and the authors are not aware of work modeling turn-taking in textual chats. [5]
In multi-agent coordination, law-governed approaches include Minsky's Law-Governed Interaction model, the Electronic Institution with roles, norms and scenes, and the XMLaw/M-Law framework, which intercepts messages and blocks non-compliant ones. [6][7][8]
Architectures are classified as rule-oriented, data-oriented, or a mix; rule-oriented examples include ELIZA and PARRY, with knowledge bases and logic (e.g., Prolog, FOL) as the basis for most rule-oriented chatbots. [9][10][11]
Data-oriented architectures learn from dialogue samples using methods such as information retrieval, neural networks, HMMs and POMDP; examples include Cleverbot and Tay, and Microsoft published an RCNN-based multi-turn multi-task SLU approach. [12][13]
A.L.I.C.E. exemplifies the mixed rule-and-data approach: its AIML knowledge is refined through incremental/interactive supervised learning, with roughly 41,000 categories. [14][15]
By intention type, systems are goal-driven/task-oriented (using POMDP, HMM, Memory Networks, with the difficulty of collecting large annotated task-specific corpora) or non-goal-driven/reactive (using RNNs, Dynamic Context-Sensitive Generation, Memory Networks, and also HTMM). [16][17][18]
For context reasoning, most state-of-the-art approaches rely on rules with logics and knowledge bases (e.g., FOL inference, triple/RDF stores such as Rya with SPARQL), while data-oriented work uses neural networks such as Memory Networks to predict the next utterance from context. [19][20][21]
Sukhbaatar's memory-network model encodes temporal context and answers context questions, but it has not been tested for goal-oriented systems and works with sentences not necessarily from multi-party bots. [22]
